title: Tenant policy middleware for jurisdictional residency routing & allow/deny lists
creator: Sofia Martinez
description:
Background: Several enterprise customers require hard enforcement of jurisdictional constraints (data residency and region-only processing) while others want per-tenant allow/deny overrides for routing specific request classes. Current routing layers implement region selection and fallback, but enforcement is scattered across the control plane and runtime, leading to inconsistent behavior during capacity shortage and canary rollouts.

Objective: Build a tenant-scoped policy middleware that centralizes residency rules, tenant allowlists/denylists, and precedence semantics. The middleware will provide a single decision API consumed by the router, admission layer, and Dedicated control-plane for deterministic routing behavior across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope:
- Core policy model: tenant residency requirement (e.g., EU-only), explicit allowlist and denylist for upstream regions/models, and emergency-exempt flags for support operations.
- Decision API: gRPC + HTTP endpoints returning explicit routing decisions with reason codes (e.g., RESIDENCY_BLOCKED, ALLOWLIST_OVERRIDE, FALLBACK_ALLOWED).
- Enforcement hooks: router policy plugin, admission validator for dedicated capacity allocations, and a migration shim for Private control plane.
- Safety: circuit-breaker when decision service is unavailable (fail-closed vs fail-open configurable per tenant), audit logging for every decision, and rate limits to protect the service.

Non-goals: building a new UI for tenant rules (Console work is a follow-up), policy authoring UX, and automatic translation of legal terms to rules (this ticket expects policy input from Legal/PM).

Trade-offs considered:
- Centralized policy service increases coupling but simplifies correctness and observability.
- Fail-closed reduces data egress risk but may cause higher error rates; we will make fail-mode tenant-configurable and instrumented.
- Keeping allow/deny lists per-tenant (versus org-wide) adds storage and caching complexity but is necessary for large customers with bespoke needs.

Acceptance criteria: see acceptance_criteria field for explicit checks.
acceptance_criteria: Decision API returns deterministic routing outcomes for tenant requests including reason code and timestamp.
Router plugin consults policy middleware and honors residency blocks and allowlist overrides during normal and degraded operation.
Configurable fail-mode per tenant (fail-closed, fail-open) is persisted and obeyed by the router.
Audit logs for policy decisions are emitted to the observability pipeline with tenant, rule-id, and decision reason.
Unit and integration tests covering: residency block, allowlist override, denylist block, emergency-exempt flow, and service unavailability behavior.
Performance: median decision latency < 5ms with 99th percentile < 25ms under expected load and cold-cache conditions.
Migration: existing tenant residency tags are reconciled; no customer sees unexpected routing changes after rollout (validated via canary with a small subset of tenants).
implementation_notes:
High-level design: lightweight policy store (Postgres + Redis caching) with a thin decision layer in Go. Policy schema: tenant_id, rule_id, rule_type (residency/allow/deny), scope (model/tier/region), precedence, emergency_exempt. Decision evaluation order: explicit denylist -> residency hard requirement -> allowlist overrides -> fallback tier rules.

Caching: shard-by-tenant LRU caches with TTL and subscription for config changes (pubsub).

Observability: attach request_id, tenant_id, rule_ids applied to traces and emit metrics: policy_decisions_total{result=blocked|allowed|fallbacked}, policy_decision_latency_ms.

Security: all policy write operations authenticated via SSO + RBAC; all decision requests require service-to-service mTLS.

Migration steps: export current residency tags, run reconciliation job to create per-tenant policies in the new store, start router plugin in read-only decision mode, run canary with 2% of tenants with monitoring, then flip enforcement on in waves.
rollout_plan: 1) Deploy policy-service v1 to staging; run synthetic traffic and validate latency and correctness. 2) Deploy router plugin to canary fleet pointing at staging service for 48h. 3) Migrate 2% of production tenants to consult mode (audit-only) and validate no denied requests where not expected. 4) Enable enforcement for canary tenants; monitor SLOs and support queues for 72h. 5) Gradually increase enforcement to 25%, 50%, 100% using automated rollout with manual pause on error thresholds. 6) Post-rollout: run reconciliation sweep and add Console UI follow-up ticket for policy editing.
